segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I'm Beth.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Smell-o-vision, a television which allows you to smell things as well as see them,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: and a miracle pill which cures all diseases.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: These predictions for the future were made in the 1930s, but so far they haven't come true.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Making predictions for the future isn't easy. Just ask tech billionaire Elon Musk, who recently predicted that artificial intelligence will eventually mean that no one will have to work.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In fact, there have been many predictions about the future of work. For example, that robots will take over most jobs and that everyone will work from home.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: During Covid, one of these predictions came true. Millions were forced to work from home.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So what will work be like in the future? That's what we'll be discussing in this programme

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: and as usual we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary too.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But first I have a question for you, Beth. Another idea for the future is the four-day working week

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: where employees work four days for the same money as five.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: After Covid, many British companies gave the idea a go.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But out of the 60 companies taking part in a four-day working week trial in 2023,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: how many said they planned to continue with a shorter work week Was it a 52 b 72 or c 92

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I guess 52% of the companies plan to continue with a four-day week.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK, Beth, I'll reveal the answer later in the programme.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Now, whatever Elon Musk thinks, as we've seen, it's difficult to make your predictions accurate.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here's Sean Lay, presenter of BBC World Service programme The Real Story,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: asking University of Cambridge professor Brendan Burchell

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: what he thinks about predictions for the future of work.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Brendan Burchell, when you look at all the predictions that have been made,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: certainly in your working lifetime,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: do you kind of take some of the things that are being predicted now

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: with a large pinch of salt?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I do. I think we have to be sceptical.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I think the track record for economists and other social scientists isn't good.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: When we look for hundreds of years, 100 years now, people have been predicting that there'll be really quite dramatic reductions in working time, like Elon Musk has just made.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And previously, those predictions, although we're heading very gradually in that direction, those predictions of very, very large changes in working time just haven't come to pass.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Sean asks if we should take predictions with a pinch of salt.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: To take something with a pinch of salt is an idiom meaning to doubt that what you've been told is accurate or likely to come true.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: For example if your friend always lies you take what they say with a pinch of salt

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Professor Birchall thinks predictions for the future of work have a bad track record

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: A track record means all the achievements or failures that someone has had in the past.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: When it comes to predicting the future of work, most predictions simply haven't come to pass an old-fashioned way of saying happened or come true.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So are predictions for a future of leisure, relaxing by the pool while robots do all the work, just a dream?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Let's hear from Andrew Palmer, business editor for The Economist magazine, talking to BBC World Service programme The Real Story.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I'm not a tech dystopian. I don't think that machines or AI are going to get rid of all jobs.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: but I do worry about a sequencing risk.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So there will be some disruption from AI.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Some jobs, some professions are at risk.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And although economists like to say new jobs will crop up,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: they won't necessarily be aligned at the same time.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: There won't be coordination.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Andrew is not a dystopian,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: someone who imagines a nightmarish future of suffering and injustice.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: He doesn't think AI will get rid of all jobs.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: To get rid of something means to remove it because you no longer want it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Andrew predicts that AI will replace some jobs, and those workers will need support.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But he also thinks new jobs will crop up. They will appear unexpectedly.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And that exactly the problem The future is hard to predict because it so unexpected Anyway I reckon a shorter working week is something we can all agree on right Neil

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Absolutely. I think it's time to reveal the answer to my question

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: about the 60 companies trying out a shorter working week in 2023.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I asked how many of them plan to continue a four-day week at the end of the trials.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I guessed 52%, so was I right?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: That was the wrong answer, I'm afraid, Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Actually, a whopping 92% of the companies plan on keeping a four-day week

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: because it was so popular with bosses as well as workers.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Right, let's recap the vocabulary we've learned from this programme,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: starting with the idiom, take it with a pinch of salt,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: meaning don't completely believe what you are told is true.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A track record means the achievements or failures of someone's past performance.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Come to pass is an old-fashioned way of saying take place or happen.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A dystopian is someone who foresees a nightmarish future

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: where there's great suffering and injustice in society.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If you get rid of something, you remove something that you no longer want.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And finally, if something crops up, it appears or happens unexpectedly.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Join us again soon for more trending topics and useful vocabulary.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: here at 6 Minute English.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Goodbye for now.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Goodbye.
